era: First teacher sent to Madinah — Martyr of Uhud
teaser: The best-dressed young man in Makkah was buried in a cloak too short to cover both ends of him.
quran_mention: The ayah the Prophet ﷺ recited standing over his body: «مِّنَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ رِجَالٌ صَدَقُوا مَا عَاهَدُوا اللَّهَ عَلَيْهِ» — 'Among the believers are men true to what they promised Allah' (33:23)

layers.title: Who He Was
layers.subtitle: The most fragrant man in Makkah
layers.content:
Mus'ab al-Khayr ibn Umayr, of Banu Abd ad-Dar ibn Qusayy — the clan that held the banner of Quraysh. His kunya was Abu Muhammad. His mother was Khannas bint Malik, and she was rich.

Ibrahim al-Abdari's report from his father is a portrait of a spoiled and much-loved boy: handsome, wealthy, young, and adored by both his parents. His mother dressed him in the best and finest clothes there were. He was the most fragrant of the people of Makkah and he wore fine Hadrami sandals. Elsewhere in the same volume he is described as having fine skin and beautiful hair, and being neither short nor tall.

The Prophet ﷺ himself once said of him — and this is preserved as a judgement on the Makkan Mus'ab, not the later one — 'I have not seen in Makkah anyone with more beautiful hair, or a finer cloak, or more blessed than Mus'ab ibn Umayr.'

His friend Amir ibn Rabi'a, who knew him from the day he became Muslim until the day he died, added the thing that is easier to miss: 'I did not see a more handsome man, or one less inclined to argue, than him.'

He had one daughter, Zaynab, whose mother was Hamna bint Jahsh.
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III, trans. Aisha Bewley (Ibrahim ibn Muhammad al-Abdari from his father; Abdullah ibn Amir ibn Rabi'a from his father)

layers.title: The Conversion
layers.subtitle: His mother tried to buy him back with pity
layers.content:
He heard that a man was calling people to Islam in the house of al-Arqam. He went, and he believed, and then he walked back out and told nobody — hiding it out of fear of his mother and his clan while slipping away to the Prophet ﷺ in secret. Uthman ibn Talha noticed where he was going and reported him. His own family seized him and locked him up. He stayed imprisoned until the first migration to Abyssinia, and Amir ibn Rabi'a records that he went on both crossings.

He came back to a Makkah that had hardened, and to a mother who withdrew from him as a reproach. The money stopped.

Years later, when he returned to Makkah with the Ansar, he went to the Prophet ﷺ first and did not go near his own house. His mother sent word: disobedient child, you come to a town I am in and do not come to me first. He answered that he would not begin with anyone before the Messenger of Allah. Then he went to her. Have you changed your religion again. 'I follow the deen of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.' Are you not grateful for the pity I showed you — once over Abyssinia and once over Yathrib. She moved to imprison him again and he said he would fight whoever came at him, and told her to go about her business. She began to weep. He said: mother, I am advising you and I have compassion for you — testify that there is no god but Allah. She refused, and said she would leave him to his religion and keep her own.
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III (Ibrahim ibn Muhammad al-Abdari from his father; Abdullah ibn Abi Bakr ibn Muhammad ibn Amr ibn Hazm)

layers.title: With the Prophet ﷺ
layers.subtitle: One man sent to convert a city
layers.content:
After the twelve men of the first Aqaba went home and Islam began moving through the houses of the Ansar, they wrote to the Prophet ﷺ and asked him to send someone who could teach them understanding of the deen and how to recite the Qur'an. He sent Mus'ab.

Al-Bara ibn Azib remembered the arrival: the first of the Companions to reach us were Mus'ab ibn Umayr and Ibn Umm Maktum. He lodged with As'ad ibn Zurara, and by another report with Sa'd ibn Mu'adh. Then he went out into the houses and the tribes, one at a time, inviting them and reciting to them. One or two men would accept. Then one or two more. It went on that way until Islam had appeared in all the houses of the Ansar and al-Awali, except a few houses of Aws Allah.

The day the chief converted is dated to the hour. Usayd ibn al-Hudayr and Sa'd ibn Mu'adh both became Muslim at Mus'ab's hands on the same day, Usayd an hour before Sa'd. Abbad ibn Bishr and Muhammad ibn Maslama had come in before them.

He wrote asking permission to assemble them, and the instruction came back: look for the day the Jews prepare for their Sabbath, and when the sun declines, draw near to Allah with two rak'ats and address them. He gathered twelve men in the house of Sa'd ibn Khaythama and one sheep was slaughtered. It was the first Jumu'ah prayer in Islam.
layers.hadith_ref: Narrated by al-Bara ibn Azib: 'The first of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to come to us were Mus'ab ibn Umayr and Ibn Umm Maktum' — Ibn Sa'd Tabaqat Vol. III
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III (a composite of chains including az-Zuhri, Yazid ibn Ruman and Waqid ibn Amr ibn Sa'd ibn Mu'adh); Ibn Sa'd notes that some of the Ansar said As'ad ibn Zurara was the first to gather them

layers.title: The Trial
layers.subtitle: He would not let the banner fall
layers.content:
He led the seventy Ansar down to the second Aqaba himself, and stayed with the Prophet ﷺ in Makkah through the rest of Dhu al-Hijjah, Muharram and Safar, then went ahead to Madinah twelve days before him. At Badr the banner of the Muhajirun was in his hand, and Ibn Sa'd's source calls it the greatest banner of the Messenger of Allah that day.

At Uhud he carried the banner again. When the Muslim lines broke and men ran, he stood still with it. Ibn Qami'a came at him on horseback and cut off his right hand. Mus'ab is reported to have said, 'Muhammad is only a Messenger, and Messengers have passed away before him.' He took the banner in his left hand. The rider bore down and cut off the left hand too. Mus'ab leaned into the staff and held it against his chest with his arms, saying it again. The third pass was a thin spear that went through him. He fell, and the banner fell with him.

Two men of his own clan rushed for it — Suwaybit ibn Sa'd and Abu ar-Rum ibn Umayr, Mus'ab's brother. Abu ar-Rum kept it in his hand until he carried it back into Madinah.

Ibn Sa'd prints an objection beside this account rather than smoothing it over. Ibrahim ibn Muhammad reports from his father that the ayah Mus'ab is quoted as reciting was not revealed on that day, but afterwards.
layers.quran_ref: Quran 3:144 — 'Muhammad is only a Messenger, and Messengers have passed away before him'
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III (Ibrahim ibn Muhammad ibn Shurahbil al-Abdari from his father; and the same chain's caveat on the timing of the ayah)

layers.title: The Legacy
layers.subtitle: Nothing left to bury him in
layers.content:
The Prophet ﷺ stood over him where he lay face down and recited: among the believers are men true to what they promised Allah. Then he said, 'The Messenger of Allah bears witness that you are martyrs with Allah on the Day of Rising.' Then he turned to the living: visit them, go to them, greet them — by the One who holds my soul, no one will greet them from now until the Day of Rising without their returning the greeting.

Khabbab ibn al-Aratt is the one who tells the hardest part. We emigrated with the Messenger of Allah seeking the face of Allah, he said, and some of us went without consuming any of the reward here — Mus'ab among them. He was killed at Uhud and there was nothing left to shroud him in but a mantle. Put it over his head and his feet showed. Put it over his feet and his head showed. The Prophet ﷺ said: put it over his head, and lay the idhkhir plant on his feet. Ibn Sa'd narrates the same shortage over Hamzah's body on the same day; there were few cloths and many dead.

Standing over him in that worn cloak, the Prophet ﷺ said, 'I saw you in Makkah and there was no one with a finer robe or more beautiful hair than you. Then you were dishevelled in a cloak.' He was around forty. His brother Abu ar-Rum, Amir ibn Rabi'a and Suwaybit went down into the grave with him.

He is not remembered for what he gave up. He is remembered because a city he was sent to alone was Muslim before the Prophet ﷺ ever set foot in it.
layers.quran_ref: Quran 33:23 — 'Among the believers are men true to what they promised Allah'
layers.hadith_ref: Narrated by Khabbab ibn al-Aratt, through Shaqiq and al-A'mash — Ibn Sa'd Tabaqat Vol. III
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III (Ubayd ibn Umayr; Khabbab ibn al-Aratt; Ibrahim ibn Muhammad ibn Shurahbil al-Abdari from his father)

quiz.prompt: How is Mus'ab described in Makkah before Islam took everything from him?

options.text: A poor orphan of Quraysh
A wealthy, handsome young man, the most fragrant person in Makkah
A merchant who traded with Syria
A poet employed by Quraysh

quiz.citation: Ibrahim ibn Muhammad al-Abdari from his father — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: His mother was rich and dressed him in the finest clothes available. The Prophet ﷺ said he had not seen anyone in Makkah with more beautiful hair or a finer cloak.

quiz.prompt: What did Mus'ab's family do when they discovered he had become Muslim?

options.text: They disowned him publicly and let him go
They imprisoned him, and he stayed locked up until the migration to Abyssinia
They followed him into Islam
They paid Quraysh to protect him

quiz.scholar_reflection: Uthman ibn Talha spotted him going to the Prophet ﷺ in secret and informed his mother and his people. He went on both migrations to Abyssinia.

quiz.prompt: Why was Mus'ab sent to Madinah before the Hijrah?

options.text: To negotiate a treaty with the Jewish tribes
To buy land for the mosque
Because the Ansar wrote asking for someone to teach them the deen and the Qur'an
To escape his mother

quiz.citation: Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat Vol. III — composite of chains including az-Zuhri and Yazid ibn Ruman
quiz.scholar_reflection: He went house to house, tribe by tribe, gaining one or two men at a time, until Islam had spread through nearly all the houses of the Ansar. Usayd ibn al-Hudayr and Sa'd ibn Mu'adh both accepted Islam at his hands in a single day.

quiz.prompt: What first is attributed to Mus'ab in the house of Sa'd ibn Khaythama?

options.text: The first Jumu'ah prayer in Islam, with twelve men present
The first Eid prayer
The first written copy of the Qur'an
The first call to prayer

quiz.citation: Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat Vol. III; Ata, through Ibn Jurayj, confirms it was a man of Banu Abd ad-Dar at the Prophet's command, and Sufyan names Mus'ab
quiz.scholar_reflection: The written instruction was to watch for the day the Jews prepared for their Sabbath, and to gather at the declining of the sun for two rak'ats and an address. One sheep was slaughtered.

quiz.prompt: What was Mus'ab shrouded in after Uhud?

options.text: Three white garments brought from Madinah
The Prophet's own cloak
A single mantle too short to cover his head and feet at once
Nothing — he was buried as he was

quiz.citation: Narrated by Khabbab ibn al-Aratt — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: The Prophet ﷺ told them to cover his head and lay the idhkhir plant over his feet. Ibn Sa'd records the identical shortage over Hamzah's body that day: few cloths, many dead.

quiz.prompt: The companions lowered their heads out of pity when they saw what Mus'ab was wearing. How do you handle being pitied?

options.text: I would rather not be seen at all
I can take it from people who love me
It stings more than the loss itself
I have never had far enough to fall to know

quiz.citation: Reflection on the report of Urwa ibn az-Zubayr through Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, Ibn Sa'd Tabaqat Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: He walked in wearing a piece of mantle patched together with a strip of leather, greeted the gathering, and the Prophet ﷺ returned the greeting and praised him. The pity was in the room; the shame was not.

quiz.prompt: His mother wept and he still would not soften on the one thing. Where is your own line?

options.text: I have one and I have had to use it
I bend for family, almost always
I keep the line and hide it from them
I do not know where mine is yet

quiz.citation: Reflection on the exchange between Mus'ab and Khannas bint Malik, Ibn Sa'd Tabaqat Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: Notice what he did with the refusal. He did not curse her or cut her off. 'Mother, I am giving you good advice and I am compassionate to you.' She kept her religion and he kept his, and he went on visiting.

quiz.prompt: He converted a city one or two men at a time. What is your instinct about scale?

options.text: I want the result to be visible or I lose heart
I trust slow work and it suits me
I would have gone for the chief first
I overestimate how fast things should move

quiz.citation: Reflection on Mus'ab's mission in Madinah, Ibn Sa'd Tabaqat Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: The chiefs did come — Usayd and Sa'd ibn Mu'adh, in one day. But Abbad ibn Bishr and Muhammad ibn Maslama were Muslim before them, and the houses were being worked through long before the day that gets remembered.

quiz.prompt: Ibn Sa'd prints the objection that the verse Mus'ab is quoted reciting came later. What do you want from a source?

options.text: I want the clean version and I admit it
The doubt printed alongside makes me trust it more
I would rather not know how the sausage is made
I want to be taught how to weigh it myself

quiz.citation: Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat Vol. III — Ibrahim ibn Muhammad from his father, on the timing of Quran 3:144
quiz.scholar_reflection: A compiler who wanted a legend would have deleted the objection. Ibn Sa'd left it two lines below the story it undercuts. That habit is why the material can be read at all.

quiz.prompt: The Prophet ﷺ said no one will greet the martyrs of Uhud without their returning the greeting. What does that change for you?

options.text: It makes the dead feel closer than I expected
I find it difficult to hold in my mind
It makes me want to say the greeting properly
I want to understand it before I feel anything about it

quiz.citation: Narrated by Ubayd ibn Umayr — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: He said it standing over Mus'ab, who was lying face down, after reciting that among the believers are men true to what they promised Allah. Then he turned to the living and told them to go and visit.
